4700:
"Doddery" describes a person — almost always an elderly one — who moves in a slow, shaky, and unsteady way. Think of someone who shuffles rather than walks, whose hands tremble slightly, and who looks as though they might lose their balance with each step. Their body seems weak and fragile, like they need to hold onto the wall or furniture to keep from falling.

If you picture a very old man making his way across a room — slow, wobbly, slightly hunched, reaching for support — that image is the heart of "doddery."

"Doddery" isn't only about how someone walks. It also carries a hint that the person's mind may be a little slow or confused — not necessarily senile, but perhaps not as sharp as they once were. Someone doddery might forget what they were saying mid-sentence, take a long time to understand something, or react to things sluggishly.

However, the physical unsteadiness is always the primary idea. The mental slowness is a secondary suggestion that may or may not be implied, depending on context.

"Doddery" is not a neutral, clinical word like "frail" or "infirm." It has a mildly informal, slightly dismissive flavour. Used about a stranger, it can sound a little unkind. Used about a beloved grandparent, it can feel affectionate, even endearing — the way you might teasingly describe someone you love. Used in a professional or political context ("a doddery old minister"), it suggests the person is past their prime and no longer fit for the role.

So the feeling it conveys depends heavily on who is saying it and about whom. It is never a compliment, but it ranges from gentle teasing to gentle contempt.

"Doddery" almost exclusively describes people, and almost always old people. You would not typically call a young person doddery unless you were being sarcastic — for example, if a young friend stumbled around clumsily after a long night, you might jokingly call them "doddery." But outside of humour, it belongs firmly in the territory of old age.

It is a moderately strong descriptor. Calling someone doddery means their unsteadiness is clearly visible and noticeable — not a subtle wobble, but the kind of frailty that makes people around them worried or cautious. It is not as harsh as "decrepit" (which sounds almost broken-down) but it is stronger than simply "a bit unsteady."

• Tottering — similar, focuses on the near-falling quality of the movement
  • Frail — weaker and more neutral; describes the body, not the movement
  • Infirm — formal and clinical; covers all kinds of physical weakness
  • Shuffling — describes the specific movement (dragging feet) but not the full picture
  • Sprightly / spry — the opposite; an elderly person who is energetic and nimble is "spry," the direct antidote to doddery

• "The doddery old professor gripped the lectern tightly as he spoke, his voice wavering."
  • "She was worried about her doddery neighbour living alone — one bad fall could be serious."
  • "Don't let his doddery appearance fool you; his mind is still razor-sharp."
  • "The committee was run by a group of doddery executives who hadn't kept up with the times."

If someone is doddery, they are physically weak, slow, and unsteady on their feet in the way that old age sometimes brings — shuffling, shaking, fragile-looking — and possibly a little mentally sluggish too. It is an informal word, slightly unkind in tone, and belongs almost entirely to descriptions of elderly people.
4701:
To dodge something means to avoid it — quickly, cleverly, or both.

The thing you're avoiding could be coming at your body (a ball, a punch), or it could be something less physical that you simply don't want to deal with (a question, a responsibility, a person). In both cases, the spirit of the word is the same: something is headed your way, and you get out of its way — or wriggle away from it.

1. Physical Dodging — Moving Your Body to Avoid Something

This is the most literal sense. You dodge when something is coming at you and you move — usually quickly and sideways — to avoid being hit or caught.

  • A boxer dodges a punch by leaning away at the last second.
  • A child dodges a ball thrown at them in a game.
  • A cyclist dodges a pothole on the road.
  • You dodge between cars to cross a busy street.

The key feeling here is: something is flying or moving toward you, and you use quick, nimble movement to escape it. It often implies speed and a kind of agility.

2. Figurative Dodging — Avoiding Something Inconvenient or Uncomfortable

This is where "dodge" is used most often in everyday conversation. Here, you're not moving your body — you're avoiding something mentally, socially, or professionally. You're escaping from a situation, a responsibility, or a conversation you don't want to face.

  • A politician dodges a journalist's question by changing the topic.
  • An employee dodges blame by pointing the finger at someone else.
  • Someone dodges their responsibilities by making excuses.
  • A student dodges difficult assignments by pretending to be sick.

In this sense, dodging almost always involves a degree of cunning or cleverness — you're not just refusing outright, you're slipping away sideways, giving a vague answer, or deflecting attention elsewhere.

This is important: dodge carries a slightly negative feeling, especially in its figurative use.

When you say someone "dodged a question" or "dodged their responsibility," you're implying that they should have faced it honestly, but instead they cleverly wriggled out of it. There's a hint of dishonesty, cowardice, or self-interest. It suggests the person was being evasive on purpose — not simply forgetting or being unable to answer, but actively avoiding.

Compare:

  • "He didn't answer the question." — neutral, no judgment.
  • "He dodged the question." — implies he deliberately avoided it, probably because the honest answer would have been inconvenient for him.

So when you use "dodge," you're often quietly accusing someone of running away from something they should have been honest about.

Dodge the question — To avoid answering a question directly by giving a vague, misleading, or off-topic response.

"Every time the interviewer asked about the financial losses, the CEO dodged the question."

Dodge responsibility / dodge blame — To avoid being held accountable for something.

"He managed to dodge all the blame even though the project failed because of his poor planning."

Dodge a bullet (idiom) — To narrowly escape a situation that could have been very bad for you. The "bullet" is a metaphor for danger or disaster.

"We dodged a bullet when we decided not to invest in that company — it went bankrupt a month later."
"She didn't get on that train, which later derailed. She really dodged a bullet."

This idiom is extremely common in casual English and simply means: you almost ended up in serious trouble, but luckily you avoided it.

Dodge traffic — To navigate through moving vehicles by changing direction or timing.

"He dodged traffic on his bicycle to reach the office faster."

Understanding a word deeply means knowing how it's different from its close cousins.

Avoid is the broadest word — it simply means to stay away from something or not do something. It says nothing about how you avoid it. "She avoided caffeine after 6pm." It's neutral and very general.

Dodge is more specific: it implies a quick or clever escape, usually from something that is already happening or coming at you. And it carries that slight negative flavour of being evasive rather than straightforwardly refusing.

Evade is very close to dodge in meaning, but it sounds more formal and more sustained. You "evade" taxes (over a long period, systematically). You "evade" capture (for days or weeks). Evade often appears in legal or official contexts, and feels more deliberate and calculated than dodge.

Duck (in its figurative sense) also means to avoid something, but it often implies a quick, momentary escape from something unpleasant — "he ducked the issue" means he briefly avoided dealing with it. It can also mean physically crouching down to avoid something.

Sidestep means to step around something rather than through it — it often applies to issues or problems and implies a smooth, polished avoidance. A politician might "sidestep" a controversy. It's slightly more elegant-sounding than dodge.

Dodge is about quick, clever avoidance — whether physical or not. It paints a picture of something coming at you and you slipping out of its way at the last moment. When used about people's behaviour (dodging questions, responsibility, blame), it quietly tells you that they were being evasive — that they ran away from something they should have faced. The word captures both the motion of avoidance and the character of the person doing it.
4702:
At the heart of "dodgy" is one simple feeling: you can't fully trust it. Whether it's a person, a thing, a place, a situation, or even food — if something is dodgy, it gives you a sense of unease, suspicion, or doubt. Something feels off about it.

"Dodgy" is primarily a British English word. You'll hear it constantly in everyday British speech. Australians and New Zealanders use it too. If you're familiar with American English, the closest equivalents are "sketchy," "shady," or "fishy" — but "dodgy" is its own flavour.

1. Dishonest, suspicious, or untrustworthy (about a person or their behaviour)

When a person is described as dodgy, it means they seem morally questionable — like they might be lying, cheating, or doing something illegal or unethical. You don't have hard proof, but something about them makes you uneasy.

"I wouldn't lend him money. He's a dodgy bloke."
"That salesman gave me a dodgy feeling — he kept avoiding my questions."
"There's something dodgy about how he made all that money so quickly."

This is the meaning that comes closest to words like shady, untrustworthy, suspicious, or crooked.

2. Of poor quality, unreliable, or faulty (about objects or services)

When a thing is dodgy, it doesn't work properly or can't be depended on. It might work sometimes and fail other times, or it might just be badly made.

"My old laptop has a dodgy keyboard — some keys don't respond."
"The Wi-Fi in this café is a bit dodgy today."
"We hired a dodgy plumber and now the pipe is leaking again."

Here, "dodgy" is close to words like unreliable, faulty, defective, or temperamental.

3. Risky, unsafe, or potentially dangerous (about a situation or place)

A dodgy situation is one where things could easily go wrong — it feels unstable, dangerous, or uncertain. A dodgy place or area is one where you don't feel safe.

"Don't walk alone in that part of town at night — it gets pretty dodgy."
"The weather looks a bit dodgy for a hike. Let's wait and see."
"It was a dodgy situation — one wrong move and everything could have gone badly."

Here it's close to risky, unsafe, precarious, or dicey.

4. Questionable or of doubtful integrity (about deals, schemes, or practices)

When a plan, deal, or business practice is dodgy, it sits in a grey area — possibly illegal, probably unethical, or at least something that wouldn't hold up under scrutiny.

"He got involved in some dodgy business dealings abroad."
"That investment scheme sounds pretty dodgy to me."
"The company had some dodgy accounting practices."

This overlaps with meaning #1, but focuses on actions and arrangements rather than a person's character directly. Close synonyms: dubious, questionable, shady, underhand.

"Dodgy" is also very commonly used for food that might have gone off (gone bad) or might make you ill. It's not necessarily obviously rotten — it's food you're not quite sure about.

"Don't eat that chicken — it smells a bit dodgy."
"I think I ate something dodgy last night. I've been feeling ill all day."

You'll very often hear "a bit dodgy" rather than just "dodgy." This is classic British understatement — saying something is a bit dodgy often means it's actually quite bad or quite suspicious. It softens the statement while making the same point.

"The wiring in this old house is a bit dodgy" — could mean it's genuinely dangerous.
"That whole situation was a bit dodgy" — could mean it was clearly corrupt.

Don't be misled by the "a bit" — the concern is real.

Even though "dodgy" covers so many situations, all its meanings share the same underlying thread:

You sense that something isn't right, isn't safe, or isn't what it appears to be.

  • A dodgy person → can't be trusted morally.
  • A dodgy object → can't be relied on to work.
  • A dodgy place or situation → can't be considered safe.
  • A dodgy deal or scheme → can't be considered honest or legal.
  • Dodgy food → can't be considered safe to eat.

The word captures that feeling of vague but real suspicion — you may not be able to point to exactly what's wrong, but your instincts are telling you to be careful.

"Dodgy" is an informal word. You'd use it in casual conversation, not in formal writing like a report or an official letter. That said, it's extremely common in British everyday speech — newspapers, TV, casual emails, text messages, conversations with friends — so you'll encounter it constantly.

It's never an extremely harsh insult. Calling someone dodgy is a warning, not an attack. It signals caution rather than outright accusation.

SituationWhat "dodgy" means
A personUntrustworthy, probably dishonest
An objectUnreliable, faulty, poorly made
A place or situationUnsafe, risky, unstable
A deal or schemeQuestionable, likely dishonest or illegal
FoodPossibly gone bad, might make you sick

The single word you can always fall back on: if something is dodgy, something about it isn't right — and your instinct is telling you to be wary.
4703:
To doff something means to take it off or to remove it — most often a hat, but also other items of clothing or gear.

Think of it as the act of lifting or pulling something off your body. Simple as that. But there's more texture to it, which you'll see below.
The Classic Use: Doffing a Hat

The most traditional and common use of "doff" is with a hat. When a person doffs their hat, they remove it — typically as a sign of respect, politeness, or greeting toward someone.

For example:

  • He doffed his hat when the funeral procession passed.
  • The gentleman doffed his cap to the woman as she walked by.

In older times, removing your hat was a social gesture. It signaled humility, acknowledgment, or honor toward another person. So "doffing a hat" was never just about the physical act — it carried social meaning.
Broader Use: Any Clothing or Gear

"Doff" isn't limited to hats. It can apply to any item you remove from your body.

  • The miners doffed their helmets at the end of the shift.
  • She doffed her coat as soon as she stepped inside.
  • The surgeon doffed his gloves after the procedure.

Whenever something is being taken off, "doff" can be the word for it.
The Figurative Use: "Doff One's Hat to Someone"

This is where the word truly lives on in modern everyday language, even for people who've never worn a formal hat in their lives.

When you say "I doff my hat to you" (or "I doff my cap to you"), you mean:

"I deeply respect what you've done. I acknowledge your achievement. I am impressed."

It's a way of expressing admiration or tribute — even without a literal hat involved.

Examples:

  • I doff my hat to anyone who can raise three children alone while working two jobs.
  • We must doff our caps to the scientists who made this breakthrough possible.
  • She doffed her hat to her rival, acknowledging the better performance.

This figurative use is quite common and you'll encounter it often in writing, speeches, and journalism.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Doff" is not a word you'd hear in casual everyday chit-chat. It has a formal, literary, and slightly old-fashioned quality to it. You're more likely to encounter it in:

  • Books, especially historical fiction or classic literature
  • Formal writing or journalism
  • Speeches or ceremonial language
  • The figurative expression "doff one's hat/cap to"

It's not a dead word — it's alive and in use — but it belongs to a more elevated register of English. Using it in casual speech would sound deliberate and stylistic, a little theatrical even.

The direct opposite of "doff" is "don", which means to put on a piece of clothing or gear.

  • Don = put it on
  • Doff = take it off

This pair is worth knowing together. You might see sentences like:

  • The workers doffed their old uniforms and donned the new ones.

Literal meaningTo remove or take off clothing, a hat, or gear
Classic useTaking off a hat as a gesture of respect or greeting
Figurative useTo express admiration or respect toward someone ("doff one's hat to")
ToneFormal, literary, slightly old-fashioned
OppositeDon (to put on)

The most important thing to walk away with: doff = remove something, especially a hat, whether as a literal action or as a gesture of respect — and in its figurative form, it's a graceful way of paying tribute to someone's achievement.
4704: Dogged means refusing to stop or give up, no matter how hard things get. It describes a steady, grinding kind of determination — the kind that keeps a person going even when they are tired, failing, or facing something very difficult. A dogged person does not quit. They push through, again and again, without giving in.

Many words describe people who try hard — determined, persistent, motivated. So what makes dogged different?

The key is in its quality of effort. "Dogged" does not describe someone who succeeds easily or who moves fast. It describes someone who grinds through difficulty without flinching. Think of it as the difference between a sprinter and a person who walks through a storm without stopping, step by step, no matter what. That second person is dogged.

There is something almost stubborn and unflinching about the word. A dogged person does not let setbacks discourage them. They do not need inspiration or perfect conditions. They simply refuse to stop.
The Tone: Is It a Compliment?

Yes — almost always. "Dogged" is a word of deep respect and admiration. When someone calls you dogged, they are saying you have a rare and impressive quality. You kept going when most people would have stopped. It is not flashy praise. It is quiet, serious admiration for real effort.

It can, very rarely, carry a slightly critical tone — suggesting someone is so stubborn they won't change course even when they should. But in everyday use, it is overwhelmingly positive.

"Dogged" is almost always followed by a noun that describes a form of effort or attitude. The most common pairings are:

  • Dogged determination — the most common phrase; a fierce refusal to quit
  • Dogged persistence — continuing to try again and again
  • Dogged pursuit — chasing a goal relentlessly
  • Dogged effort — hard, sustained work
  • Dogged refusal — firmly, unmovably saying no
  • Dogged loyalty — sticking by someone no matter what

You will rarely see "dogged" used alone. It typically sits just before a noun, giving that noun a quality of grinding, unyielding strength.

• Her dogged determination helped her pass the exam after failing it four times.

This means: She refused to give up, even after failing repeatedly. That quality of never quitting is what carried her through.

  • The detective's dogged pursuit of the truth finally solved the case after ten years.

Here, "dogged pursuit" tells us the detective kept investigating long after others had given up.

  • Despite injury and exhaustion, his dogged refusal to leave the field inspired his whole team.

He would not stop, no matter what. That stubborn refusal was admirable.

  • It was not talent that made her successful — it was dogged hard work.

This is a powerful use of the word. It says: no shortcuts, no luck. Just relentless effort, day after day.

It is a strong word. It doesn't describe mild effort. It describes the kind of persistence that stands out — the kind that makes people take notice and feel impressed. It belongs to a higher register than simply "hardworking." When a journalist writes that a scientist showed "dogged persistence" in their research, or a coach calls a player "dogged," they mean that person showed something exceptional.

• It does not mean aggressive or loud. A dogged person is quiet, steady, and relentless — not confrontational.
  • It does not require success. Someone can be dogged and still fail. The word describes the quality of effort, not the outcome.
  • It does not mean fast. Dogged effort is often slow, patient, and grinding.
  • It is not about emotion. A dogged person is not necessarily passionate or excited. They may even feel exhausted or discouraged — but they keep going anyway. That is the point.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Picture a dog locked onto a bone. It chews and chews, ignoring everything around it. No distraction pulls it away. Nothing makes it stop. It is fully committed to that one thing for as long as it takes.

That image — unflinching, tireless, locked-in — is exactly what "dogged" means when it describes a person.
4705:
Doggedly means doing something with stubborn, relentless determination — continuing even when it is very difficult, painful, or seems hopeless.

When someone does something doggedly, they refuse to give up. They keep pushing forward no matter how many times they fail, how tired they get, or how many obstacles appear in their way.

This is not just ordinary persistence. "Doggedly" carries a special flavour — it suggests struggle. The person is not breezing through something; they are grinding through it, jaw clenched, step by step.

Think of a bulldog that bites onto something and simply will not let go, no matter what. That image captures the soul of this word perfectly: a fierce, almost stubborn refusal to quit.

So when you use "doggedly," you are saying two things at once:

  1. This person kept going.
  2. It was hard, and they kept going anyway.

Read each sentence and notice how "doggedly" changes the feeling:

  • She doggedly studied for the exam even after failing it twice.
    → She didn't give up after failing. She kept studying with determined effort.
  • The scientist doggedly pursued the cure for 20 years, despite little funding and no results.
    → He kept working for two decades through frustration and disappointment — without quitting.
  • The detective doggedly followed every clue until she finally solved the case.
    → She investigated with relentless effort, leaving nothing unexplored.
  • He doggedly climbed through the storm, step by painful step.
    → Even though it was physically brutal, he kept moving forward.
  • They doggedly defended their position in the debate, refusing to back down.
    → They held their ground stubbornly, not yielding to pressure.

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important.

"Doggedly" ≠ easily. If something came naturally or without effort, you would never use "doggedly." The word always carries the sense of fighting through difficulty.

"Doggedly" ≠ carelessly. Someone doing something doggedly is focused and purposeful. They have a goal and they are working toward it with full commitment.

"Doggedly" ≠ quickly. Doggedness is about endurance, not speed. A person doing something doggedly might be slow — but they are steady and unstoppable.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Persistently — also means "continuing without stopping," but it is emotionally flat. It just describes the action. "Doggedly" adds the feeling of struggle, stubbornness, and grit.

She persistently sent emails. (neutral, just means she kept sending)
She doggedly sent emails. (she kept sending despite being ignored, rejected, or exhausted — she refused to quit)

Stubbornly — focuses on refusing to change your mind, often negatively. "Doggedly" focuses on refusing to stop trying, which is usually admirable.

Stubborn people often won't listen to reason.
Dogged people won't stop working toward a goal.

Relentlessly — means "without ever letting up," and can feel aggressive or even threatening. "Doggedly" is warmer and more about personal endurance than pressure on others.
The Tone and When to Use It

"Doggedly" almost always carries a tone of admiration or respect. When a writer or speaker uses this word, they are usually quietly praising the person — acknowledging that what they did took real grit.

Use "doggedly" when:

  • Someone kept trying despite repeated failure
  • Someone worked on something for a very long time against the odds
  • Someone refused to give up even when others around them did
  • The struggle was real and visible, not easy

These are the other forms of the same word, so you recognise them when you see them:

  • Dogged (adjective): describing a person or effort that has this quality.
    "She was a dogged competitor." → She had relentless, stubborn determination.
  • Doggedness (noun): the quality itself.
    "His doggedness eventually paid off." → His refusal to quit eventually led to success.
  • Doggedly (adverb — the form you asked about): describes how an action is done.
    "She worked doggedly." → She worked with stubborn, tireless determination.

Doggedly = doing something with fierce, stubborn determination, continuing through difficulty without giving up.

If you remember only one thing: when someone does something doggedly, they have the spirit of a dog that bites and will not let go — no matter what.
4706:
Doggerel is a word for a specific kind of bad poetry — verse that is clumsily written, poorly crafted, and lacking real artistic skill. When someone calls a piece of writing "doggerel," they mean it as a criticism. It's not just simple poetry or short poetry — it is poetry that fails, usually because the writer was more focused on making lines rhyme than on writing something genuinely good.

Think of it this way: if poetry were cooking, doggerel would be a meal where someone threw random ingredients together just to fill a plate — technically food, but clearly made without care or skill.

Several specific flaws tend to make verse qualify as doggerel. They often appear together:

1. Forced or weak rhymes
This is the most classic sign of doggerel. The writer needs a rhyme, so they grab whatever word fits the sound — even if it makes little sense or sounds unnatural. The rhyme is clearly in charge; meaning and logic take a back seat.

For example, imagine a verse that says:
"I walked to the shop on a cold winter's day / The weather was awful in every which way."

"In every which way" is a hollow, awkward phrase. It's there purely to rhyme with "day." A skilled poet would never write it. That's doggerel thinking.

2. Stumbling, uneven rhythm
Good poetry has a rhythm you can feel — a pulse, a flow. When you read it aloud, it moves naturally. In doggerel, the rhythm lurches and stumbles. To make a line "fit," the writer might awkwardly stretch a word, squash two syllables together unnaturally, or pad a line with filler words. The result feels mechanical and clunky, like a car engine misfiring.

3. Trivial, clichéd language
Doggerel tends to rely on overused, lazy expressions and flat, unoriginal ideas. There is no freshness, no surprising image, no moment that makes you see the world differently. It simply states the obvious in the most predictable way possible.

4. The form feels like a trap, not a tool
In skilled poetry, the rhyme scheme and structure serve the meaning — they amplify what the poet is trying to say. In doggerel, it's the reverse: the poet is trapped by their chosen rhyme scheme and is contorting the language and ideas to fit it. You can sense the struggle.

Here is a short piece of doggerel (written deliberately badly to illustrate the point):

The sunshine is bright on this wonderful day,
The birds all are singing in quite a nice way,
The flowers are pretty with colours so red,
I think that I'll go now and lie on my bed.

Notice the problems:

  • "In quite a nice way" is meaningless filler — it's there only to rhyme with "day."
  • "Colours so red" is backwards and awkward — natural English says "red colours" or just "red flowers."
  • The last line has nothing to do with the rest — it's a random thought dragged in to close the rhyme.
  • The rhythm is inconsistent and bumpy when read aloud.
  • The whole thing is flat, clichéd, and tells us nothing interesting.

Now contrast that with even two lines of real, skilled verse, and the difference is immediately obvious. Skilled verse feels inevitable — like the words could not have been arranged any other way.
A Crucial Distinction: Simple Is Not the Same as Doggerel

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word. Doggerel is not simply poetry that is short, easy to read, or written for ordinary people. Many brilliant poems are short and simple. A well-crafted nursery rhyme, a sharp limerick, a witty comic verse — these can all be simple and still be excellent. The difference is craft.

Doggerel fails not because it is unpretentious or accessible, but because it is poorly made. A skilled poet can write something short, rhyming, and lighthearted — and it will not be doggerel. Doggerel is about a lack of skill, care, and craftsmanship, not about simplicity or subject matter.

Yes — and this is a subtle but interesting point. Sometimes a writer deliberately produces clunky, ridiculous verse as a joke. The badness itself becomes the comedy. Political satirists, comedians, and humourists have done this — leaning into the clumsiness on purpose to mock someone or something. In this case, the doggerel is still technically bad verse, but the writer is in full control, using badness as a tool. The key difference is intent and awareness: a skilled writer producing intentional doggerel knows exactly what they're doing and why. An unskilled writer producing accidental doggerel simply can't do better.

"Doggerel" is almost always used as a criticism, and it carries a slightly dismissive, even contemptuous tone. When someone describes a poem as doggerel, they are not being gentle. They are saying: this is poor work, this is verse that lacks real poetic ability. It can also be used humorously and self-deprecatingly — a writer might joke, "Oh, that old thing I wrote? Pure doggerel." — but even then, the meaning is the same: bad poetry.
How It Is Used in Sentences

• "The greeting card was stuffed with doggerel that made everyone at the party wince."
  • "The critic tore apart the poet's new collection, calling most of it doggerel dressed up in fancy language."
  • "He laughed and admitted that his early teenage attempts at poetry were nothing but doggerel."
  • "The campaign team asked a poet to write a slogan, but what came back was embarrassing doggerel."
  • "She could tell the difference between clever light verse and mere doggerel, and this was definitely the latter."
Doggerel is verse (poetry) that is badly and clumsily written — typically marked by forced rhymes, stumbling rhythm, and lazy language — reflecting a lack of genuine poetic skill or care.
4707:
A dogma is a belief — or a set of beliefs — that is declared to be absolutely, certainly true by some authority, and that you are expected to accept without question, without proof, and without debate.

Think of it this way: most beliefs in life are open. You can challenge them, test them, update them when new evidence comes along. A dogma is the opposite. It is presented as a fixed truth — final, non-negotiable, and beyond doubt.
Breaking It Down With an Example

Imagine a religious institution that declares:

"God created the universe in six days. This is the truth. It does not require proof. It must be believed."

That declaration is a dogma. It comes from an authority. It is stated as absolute truth. And members of that faith are expected to accept it as-is — not because they personally investigated and concluded it was true, but because the authority said so, and that is enough.
The Three Core Features of a Dogma

Every dogma tends to share these three qualities:

1. It comes from an authority.
A dogma doesn't come from your own personal reasoning. It comes from somewhere above you — a church, a political party, a powerful institution, or a dominant ideology. The authority is the source of its "truth."

2. It is presented as certain and absolute.
A dogma is not a "maybe" or a "we think." It is stated as a definite, unshakeable truth. There is no grey area, no room for "well, possibly not."

3. It is not open to questioning.
This is the sharpest edge of the word. Dogmas are not up for debate. You are expected to accept them on faith or obedience — not because logic or evidence led you there. Questioning a dogma is often seen as disloyal, heretical, or simply wrong.

In Religion

This is where the word is most commonly and most literally used. Religious dogmas are the officially declared, non-negotiable truths of a faith.

For example:

  • The dogma of the Trinity in Christianity — the belief that God is three persons in one (Father, Son, Holy Spirit). This is not presented as a theory. It is official church dogma.
  • The dogma of papal infallibility in Catholicism — the belief that when the Pope speaks officially on matters of faith, he cannot be wrong.

These are not invitations to discussion. They are declared truths.

In Politics and Ideology

Dogma is not limited to religion. Any rigid, unquestionable belief within a political movement can be called a dogma.

For example:

  • In some communist regimes, the idea that the state knows best and the individual must serve the collective was treated as dogma — a truth beyond challenge.
  • In extreme free-market thinking, the belief that the market always corrects itself and must never be interfered with can become a dogma — accepted absolutely, regardless of evidence to the contrary.

When a political belief becomes immune to facts, to counter-evidence, and to reasonable debate, it has crossed into dogma.

In Everyday Life

You'll also hear the word used informally to describe any rigid, assumed truth in a group, culture, or profession.

For example:

  • "In that company, the founder's management style was treated as dogma — nobody dared question it."
  • "For years, eating fat was seen as the enemy of health. That dogma has since been challenged by nutritional science."
The plural of dogma is dogmas (commonly used) or dogmata (the classical form, rare in everyday use). You'll almost always see dogmas in modern writing.
The Tone of the Word: Neutral or Negative?

This is important. Dogma can be used in two ways:

Neutrally — simply to describe a set of official beliefs without any judgment. Religious scholars and theologians use it this way all the time. Saying "this is a Catholic dogma" is just a factual, descriptive statement.

Negatively — to criticize a belief system for being closed-minded, rigid, or blind to evidence. When someone says "you're trapped in dogma," they are accusing you of accepting something uncritically, of refusing to think for yourself. This is the more common tone in general conversation.

The context will almost always tell you which meaning is intended.
How Dogma Differs From Similar Words

These words are close neighbors, and the differences matter:

Dogma vs. Belief
A belief is personal — something you hold to be true based on your experience, faith, or reasoning. A dogma is institutional — it is handed to you by an authority and expected to be accepted unconditionally. All dogmas are beliefs, but not all beliefs are dogmas.

Dogma vs. Opinion
An opinion is a personal, subjective view — and crucially, it is understood to be open to change. You can change your opinion after a good argument. A dogma, by definition, is not meant to change. It resists argument.

Dogma vs. Doctrine
These two are very close, and often used interchangeably, but there is a subtle difference. Doctrine is the broader body of teachings or principles that a religion or institution teaches. Dogma is a specific, officially declared, non-negotiable truth within that doctrine. Think of doctrine as the whole manual, and dogma as the parts of the manual printed in permanent ink that can never be revised.

Dogma vs. Principle
A principle is a guiding rule or value — something like "treat others fairly" or "honesty matters." Principles are usually arrived at through reasoning and are open to refinement. Dogma is more rigid, more authoritative, and more resistant to questioning.
The Big Picture: Why This Word Matters

Understanding the word dogma gives you a useful lens for the world. It helps you notice when a group, institution, or ideology has stopped reasoning and started demanding. When something is treated as sacred truth simply because an authority says so — when evidence, logic, and questioning are unwelcome — you are looking at dogma.

This doesn't automatically make something wrong. Many people live deeply meaningful lives around religious dogmas. But recognizing dogma for what it is — a belief held beyond the reach of questioning — is a mark of clear, independent thinking.

In one sentence: A dogma is an absolute, non-negotiable truth declared by an authority and expected to be accepted without question or proof.
4708:
When you call someone or something dogmatic, you mean they hold their beliefs or opinions with such strong, unshakeable certainty that they refuse to consider any other point of view — even when faced with good reasons or evidence to think differently.

A dogmatic person essentially says (not always in words, but in attitude): "I am right. This is the truth. There is nothing further to discuss."

Think of it in two parts:

1. Holding a belief very firmly — not just "I think this is probably right" but "I am completely certain this is the truth, full stop."

2. Refusing to be challenged — not open to questions, doubts, new information, or other perspectives. The matter, in their mind, is already settled.

It is the combination of both that makes something truly dogmatic. Being very confident alone isn't dogmatic. Being stubborn alone isn't dogmatic either. It's when someone is rigidly certain AND closed off to any questioning — that's dogmatic.

Imagine two teachers:

Teacher A says: "Eating breakfast is important. Here's the research behind it — though some studies do suggest it depends on the person. What do you think?"

Teacher B says: "Eating breakfast is important. That's a fact. I don't want to hear any debate about it. It's settled."

Teacher B is being dogmatic. They've locked the door on any further conversation, questioning, or new evidence. Their belief has become, in their mind, an absolute truth that cannot be touched.
Where You'll See This Word Used

Dogmatic is used in many different areas of life:

  • Religion: Someone who insists their religion is the one true religion and won't engage with any other spiritual ideas is being dogmatic.
  • Politics: A politician who rigidly sticks to their party's ideology no matter what the real-world situation demands is being dogmatic.
  • Science: A scientist who refuses to change their theory even when new evidence contradicts it is being dogmatic (this is actually considered a serious flaw in science, where changing your view based on evidence is a virtue).
  • Everyday life: A parent who says "In this family, we do things this way — no questions, no exceptions" is being dogmatic.
  • Philosophy: A thinker who accepts a set of ideas as absolutely, unquestionably true without testing or examining them is thinking dogmatically.

Dogmatic is almost always used as a criticism. When you call someone dogmatic, you are not complimenting them. You are pointing out a flaw: they are intellectually closed, arrogant in their certainty, and unwilling to learn or grow.

It implies a kind of mental stubbornness — the person has built a wall around their belief so that nothing can get in or out.

Occasionally, in very formal or academic writing, it can be used in a more neutral, descriptive way (e.g., "the dogmatic teachings of the church"), simply meaning "based on established doctrine or fixed principles" — without necessarily criticising. But in everyday modern usage, it nearly always carries a negative tone.

To sharpen the meaning, here's what it doesn't mean:

  • It does not just mean "strongly opinionated." You can have strong opinions and still be open to debate — that is not dogmatic.
  • It does not mean "passionate about a belief." Passion combined with openness is fine. Passion combined with total closed-mindedness is dogmatic.
  • It does not mean "wrong." A dogmatic person might actually hold a correct belief — but the problem is their approach: they arrived at it (or hold onto it) without genuine reasoning or openness.

• "He was so dogmatic about his diet that he refused to even listen to his doctor's advice."
  • "The professor had a dogmatic teaching style — students were expected to memorize her conclusions, not question them."
  • "Great thinkers are rarely dogmatic; they remain curious and open to being proved wrong."
  • "Her dogmatic attitude toward politics made conversations with her exhausting — she simply wouldn't consider any other perspective."

Since you might encounter these:

  • Dogmatically (adverb) — in a dogmatic manner: "He spoke dogmatically, as if the debate were already over."
  • Dogmatism (noun) — the quality or practice of being dogmatic: "His dogmatism made him a poor scientist."
  • Dogmatist (noun) — a person who is dogmatic: "She was a true dogmatist — her mind had never once been changed by an argument."
  • Dogma (noun) — a principle or set of beliefs that a group or authority declares to be absolutely true and not open to question. Dogmatic behaviour is rooted in clinging to a dogma.

Understanding opposites helps cement a word's meaning. The opposite of dogmatic is being:

  • Open-minded — willing to consider other views
  • Flexible — able to adapt your thinking
  • Empirical — basing beliefs on evidence and willing to revise them
  • Humble — acknowledging that you might be wrong

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: dogmatic describes a person or attitude that treats a belief as absolutely, unquestionably true and refuses to consider any challenge, doubt, or alternative — and this is almost always seen as a flaw.
4709:
Dogmatism is the tendency to hold your beliefs as absolutely and certainly true — and to refuse to question, examine, or reconsider them, no matter what evidence, arguments, or perspectives are presented to you.

A person who practices dogmatism (called a dogmatist) doesn't just feel confident about their beliefs. They treat their beliefs as fixed, final, and beyond all doubt — closed off from any possibility of being wrong.

Think of it this way: imagine a locked room. All the ideas inside the room are accepted as perfect truth. Any new idea trying to enter from outside — through evidence, reasoning, or someone else's experience — is simply not allowed in. That locked room is the dogmatist's mind.

To understand dogmatism deeply, you need to understand what a dogma is, because dogmatism is built on top of it.

A dogma is a principle, belief, or set of beliefs that a person (or a group) accepts as absolutely true and authoritative — not because they've fully reasoned it out themselves, but because it has been declared true by some authority (a religion, an ideology, a tradition, a leader) and is expected to be accepted without question.

Dogmatism, then, is the attitude or behavior of clinging to dogmas in a rigid, unjustified, and closed-minded way. It is not just believing something strongly — it is believing something in a way that shuts down all thinking, all questioning, and all openness to being wrong.

Three things together make a belief or an attitude dogmatic:

1. Certainty without sufficient justification.
The dogmatist is completely sure about something without having solid, well-examined reasons to be that sure. The certainty doesn't come from careful thinking — it comes from blind acceptance.

2. Refusal to question.
A dogmatist won't genuinely examine their own beliefs. They don't ask, "What if I'm wrong? What would it take to change my mind?" In fact, the very idea of questioning their belief feels threatening or even immoral to them.

3. Resistance to outside perspectives.
A dogmatist dismisses anyone who disagrees — not by engaging with their argument honestly, but by rejecting it outright. They don't say "here's why you're wrong." They say "you're simply wrong, and that's that."

Dogmatism is not confined to one area of life. It appears everywhere.

In religion: A religious dogmatist might believe that their faith's teachings are the only absolute truth in the universe and that any other belief system is completely false — without ever genuinely exploring why they believe this or seriously engaging with other viewpoints.

In politics: A political dogmatist is someone who adopts an ideology — say, a particular brand of conservatism, liberalism, or nationalism — and applies it mechanically to every issue, refusing to admit complexity, nuance, or the validity of any opposing view. Every issue gets filtered through the same fixed lens, no matter how different the issues are.

In science: This one surprises people, but even science can be practiced dogmatically. A scientist who insists on a particular theory and refuses to take contradicting evidence seriously — clinging to their idea not because the evidence supports it, but because they are personally or professionally committed to it — is being dogmatic. This is why great scientists are supposed to welcome challenges to their ideas.

In everyday life: A parent who insists "this is how it's always been done in our family, and that's the right way, period" — without reflection — is being dogmatic. So is a person who says "my generation's values are simply correct and younger generations are just wrong" without any genuine engagement with why.
Dogmatism vs. Things It's Often Confused With

This is crucial for truly understanding the word.

Dogmatism is NOT the same as having strong beliefs.
You can believe something very strongly — even passionately — and still not be dogmatic. The difference is that a non-dogmatic person, even with strong convictions, remains genuinely open to examining their beliefs, considering new evidence, and potentially revising their view. A dogmatist is not open to any of this.

Dogmatism is NOT the same as confidence.
Confidence based on solid reasoning and evidence is healthy and legitimate. A scientist who is confident that the Earth is round is not being dogmatic — there is overwhelming, testable, verifiable evidence. Dogmatism is confidence untethered from this kind of solid foundation, or confidence that refuses to even check its own foundation.

Dogmatism is NOT the same as faith.
This is a subtle distinction. Faith, in most philosophical and religious traditions, involves trusting in something beyond what you can fully prove — but it doesn't necessarily mean you've stopped thinking or that you refuse to engage with difficult questions. Many deeply faithful people are also deeply reflective, curious, and open. Dogmatism is the version of faith (or any belief) where thinking has been replaced by rigid, unexamined acceptance.
Why Is Dogmatism Considered a Flaw?

Dogmatism is almost universally regarded as an intellectual and moral problem. Here is why:

It blocks the search for truth. If you've already decided you know the truth and nothing can change your mind, you've stopped looking. But the world is complex, and our understanding grows over time. History is full of things that were once "absolutely certain" and were later proven wrong — from flat-Earth beliefs to medical practices that harmed patients. Dogmatism prevents this kind of growth.

It distorts reasoning. A dogmatist doesn't think freely. Instead, they work backward — they start with the conclusion they already believe and then selectively look for reasons to support it, ignoring everything that contradicts it. This is the opposite of good thinking.

It harms relationships and society. Dogmatism makes genuine dialogue impossible. When one person treats their position as beyond question, there is no real conversation — only one-sided declaration. At a societal level, dogmatic thinking has historically fueled intolerance, persecution, and conflict, because if your beliefs are absolutely and certainly right, then anyone who differs from you is absolutely wrong — and that's a dangerous place to be.

It is intellectually dishonest. There is a kind of humility that honest thinking requires — an acknowledgment that you might be wrong, that your perspective is limited, that you haven't seen everything. Dogmatism abandons this humility entirely.
An Important Nuance: Degrees of Dogmatism

Dogmatism isn't always extreme or obvious. It exists on a spectrum.

At one end, you have extreme dogmatism — a person who is completely sealed off from any new idea, who might even become hostile or aggressive when their beliefs are questioned, and who treats disagreement as a personal attack or a moral failure.

At the other end, you have mild or subtle dogmatism — a person who thinks they are open-minded, but in practice always finds a way to dismiss ideas that challenge their core beliefs, never truly sitting with the possibility that they could be wrong. This milder form is actually very common and much harder to detect — even in ourselves.

This is why thinkers and philosophers have long warned that dogmatism is not just a flaw in "other people." It is a temptation that everyone faces. The antidote — the opposite of dogmatism — is called critical thinking or, in philosophy, a stance of open inquiry: the genuine, ongoing willingness to examine your beliefs, question your assumptions, and follow the evidence wherever it leads, even if it's uncomfortable.

If you had to carry just one sentence to remember this word for life, let it be this:

Dogmatism is the attitude of treating your own beliefs as certainly and absolutely true, while closing your mind to any questioning, evidence, or perspective that might challenge them.
